title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
content:
I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies, a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis, and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter. I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434, aka the asinine Super Intelligence one.

First, the updated chart

Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks.

The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am.

I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version (GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau:

For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version):

In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services".

Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%.

The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here. Here's a copy of the file I used.

You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF.

The changing language of the questions

As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine):

In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement:

In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable.

From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence

When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead:

In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.)

The BTOS about page explains what happened:

Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434.

The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday.

Is this going to affect the survey?

The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results.

The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI".

I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though.

title: Audience capture
content:
Audience capture is the part that scares me the most about writing on the internet. I have the soul of an engineer1: when I see a metric like engagement, I want to improve it. I like to make the number go up.

In fact, the whole environment of online writing is tailor-made to help you make engagement numbers go up. It’s trivial to find out how many people are reading my posts, and from what sources. Hundreds of link aggregators all over the internet have algorithms that will help my most engagement-friendly posts get views, and the comments are helpfully sorted by upvotes so I can read the “best”2 pieces of feedback straight away. Many platforms are set up to financially reward you for engagement, whether that’s by enabling advertisement or by straight up paying you out.

Leaning into this environment is a huge mistake. Views and engagement are valuable to me, but not directly. They are proxy metrics for the things I actually care about:

  • Having smart, informed people read and consider my ideas
  • Getting feedback from readers who have concrete experience with the topics I write about
  • Joining interesting public conversations about the state of the industry
  • Convincing people to think like me on points I care deeply about
  • Building a reputation as a careful thinker and a good writer3

It does not benefit me at all to have ten thousand people click through to one of my posts, scan the first sentence, then close the tab. It benefits me only a little4 to have a hundred people read the title of my post on Hacker News, decide not to click through, and leave their comments in the thread. The set of people who do those things — we could call them “clickers”, as opposed to “readers” — does not really overlap with the set of people who will actually read my posts and think about them. And yet in terms of metrics and engagement, they are indistinguishable.

As with any proxy metric, optimizing it too hard can cause it to diverge from the actual value it’s targeting. This leads to the scariest form of audience capture: being captured by an audience you don’t really even want. Suppose I get a lot of views when I write posts about how stupid it is to use microservices5, because it’s a hot topic. That gives me a reason to write more posts about microservices. The numbers keep climbing. However, I suspect the set of people who read my posts thoroughly — the audience I actually care about — don’t really want to read a bunch of the same screeds about that, so they drift away6. The people clicking don’t care because they’re not reading the posts anyway. So I’m actually failing, not succeeding: I’m replacing my audience of careful thinkers with a fake audience of clickers and sneerers.

This is not just a post about writing on the internet. In 2025, I wrote Trying to impress people you don’t respect about how succeeding as an engineer involves, well, impressing people who you may not necessarily respect. The core idea here is knowing what game you’re playing. Some games are proxy games, like getting views on posts or having great Jira ticket metrics. Some games are real games, like gaining the respect of people who you respect, or doing technical work you can be proud of, or trying to convince people of things that you believe are true.

The difference is in whether you care about the goal of the game, not in whether that goal is objectively valuable. If you really want to get promoted, then that’s a real game; if you just want to do solid technical work, getting promoted might be a proxy game that you play in order to get into a position to do that. But even though you don’t really care about it, it’s easy and tempting to win the proxy game at the expense of the real game: for instance, to crush Jira tickets because they’re in front of you instead of doing what will actually get you promoted, or to get views on the internet by playing into clickbait.

Making tradeoffs like this is sometimes fine. For instance, you might decide to impress people you don’t like so you can afford to send your kids to a good school. Selling out a little bit is good and healthy7. But do it with eyes open! The absolute worst thing you can do is to sell out by habit, in situations where it doesn’t even buy you anything you want.

There are a lot of posts that I really enjoyed writing that did not get much attention: typically posts where I get a bit more into the philosophy or history, or posts that are dry technical explainers. Some of my most popular posts are laments about a changing industry that are really just popular because they give people an outlet to share their worries too, not because of anything I wrote. I think it’d be a big mistake to lean into writing more posts like that and fewer posts like this. For one, if I want to just optimize for engagement, why write blogs at all? Why not post ragebait and pornography? But the main reason is that I’m writing for the 5% of readers that will read my posts, think about them, talk to other people about the ideas, email me with their comments, and so on.

Raw view counts help expose my writing to more of those people, but they don’t give me much signal on whether I’m appealing to them or not. For that I have to just rely on my taste, or on the thin signal I get back from the readers who do email and message me with thoughtful responses.

  1. In my own terminology, an “impure engineer”.

    ↩

  2. Or at least the cleverest, or the most cutting.

    ↩

  3. Too honest? I could be even more honest and add “encouraging people to potentially hire me if I’m ever looking”, too.

    ↩

  4. Boosting engagement on Hacker News means the post is more visible for people who might actually read it.

    ↩

  5. Imagine it’s 2015 again. Go on, you know you want to.

    ↩

  6. Sunil Pai has a great post about this dynamic. To quote him: “you don’t get a notification that says, “three people respected you slightly less after reading that.” you don’t get one saying, “someone who was thinking about introducing you to somebody decided not to,” or “someone who thought you might be great to work with now thinks you seem like kind of a pain in the ass.” that stuff is completely invisible.”

    ↩

  7. If you prefer, you could call it “flexibility”.

    ↩

content:

Autodoxing (permalink)

After 25 years of fighting for human rights amid the wreckage of bad tech policy, I'm here to tell you that the road to hell is paved with badly thought-through tech policy.

The most galling thing about this wreckage is that it was both foreseeable and foreseen. Back when Sun Microsystems CEO Scott McNealy was telling the world "Privacy is dead, get over it," digital rights advocates were saying, "Not only are digital tools pretty dang good at helping you protect your privacy, but a society-wide abolition of privacy sets us up for infinite harms long into the future":

https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/31/losing-the-crypto-wars/#surveillance-monopolism

It wasn't just business leaders who hated privacy, it was also our political classes. Bill Clinton tried to put a backdoor into every microchip (no, really):

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clipper_chip

The NSA managed to enact a total prohibition on civilian access to working encryption, on the grounds that we're all safer if our spooks can spy on "bad guys" even if that means that every creep, petty crook, corporate or state-sponsored spy, and mafia can spy on us:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/04/09/bernstein-2/#win-some-lose-some

Even after that ban was overturned, governments encouraged the private sector to spy on us without limit, precaution or permission. Those private-sector troves of intimate, compromising data about every person alive constitute a warrantless, off-the-books surveillance system that cops, spies and government agencies can tap at will:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/13/petards-r-us/#nobus

To protect these surveillance capabilities, private firms and governments colluded to pass "anticircumvention" laws that make it illegal to reverse engineer our devices and apps to add privacy blockers to them, with the effect that every device we own and every app we use spies on us constantly:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/03/12/market-failure/#car-wars

At the same time, states either failed to pass new privacy laws (as in the USA, where federal consumer privacy law was last updated in 1988), or passed privacy laws that went unenforced (as in the EU, where "pretending to be Irish" allows US tech giants to flout EU privacy law):

https://pluralistic.net/2023/05/15/finnegans-snooze/#dirty-old-town

Our surveillance free-for-all world is objectively very bad. Over and over, companies and agencies who have been permitted to nonconsensually harvest and retain our data demonstrate that they are not capable of keeping that data safe, and no matter how badly they fuck up, nothing changes. It's been nearly a decade since Equifax doxed 148 million Americans and not only is the company still in business, they've been permitted to buy up and absorb more commercial surveillance firms.

US regulators let Equifax buy Teletrack in 2021. Canadian regulators let them buy the Food Industry Credit Bureau in 2023. The same year, Brazilian regulators let Equifax buy Boa Vista Serviços. This all despite the fact that Equifax blamed its breach on shitty security practices after a string of mergers that led to it haphazardly combining databases from newly acquired surveillance companies.

Data isn't the new oil. Data is the new oily rag: profitable only if you can warehouse it in vast quantities under unsafe conditions and have society pick up the bill for every conflagration:

https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-zucks-empire-of-oily-rags/

Equifax is a serial reoffender, but rather than getting the corporate death-penalty, they've been made to pay coins-down-the-back-of-the-sofa fines that amount to a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of the costs they imposed on society by amassing these vast, flaming storehouses of oily rags.

Why wouldn't Equifax reoffend? Our policymakers keep demanding less privacy, not more, and their indifference to the consequences is (almost) comical.

Take Malcolm Turnbull, the former Australian Prime Minister who uttered what remains, without a doubt, the single stupidest thing anyone anywhere has ever said about tech policy. Like many of his peers before, during, and since his reign, Turnbull had been trying to outlaw working encryption, insisting that every device have a Bill Clinton-esque back-door for the purpose of spying on "bad guys." When told that the laws of mathematics dictated that any measure that let Australia's cops spy on "bad guys" would also let bad guys spy on Australians, Turnbull replied, "The laws of mathematics are very commendable, but the only law that applies in Australia is the law of Australia":

https://www.newscientist.com/article/2140747-laws-of-mathematics-dont-apply-here-says-australian-pm/

We could laugh Turnbull off…if he was an outlier. But while Turnbull had the world's stupidest rejoinder to the scientifically irrefutable fact that banning encryption will let bad guys hack everything, he was hardly alone in wanting to ban encryption. Banning encryption is current policy in Canada:

https://blog.mozilla.org/netpolicy/2026/10/08/canadas-bill-c-22-threatens-encryption-users-privacy-and-the-security-of-digital-economies/

It's also current policy in the UK:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/03/05/theyre-still-trying-to-ban-cryptography/

And in the EU:

https://fightchatcontrol.eu/

The difference between Malcolm Turnbull and, say, Canadian PM Mark Carney is that Turnbull was stupid enough to try to defend his ban on encryption, while Carney simply shakes his head at his critics' naivete and continues to press forward with his catastrophic proposal to welcome every cybercriminal in the world to hack every morsel of Canadian data.

When it comes to bad privacy policy, our political classes aren't content to rest on their laurels: hardly a week goes by without news of a new way to encourage (or even require) the private sector to recklessly collect and retain our data, despite the dead certainty that this data will eventually end up breaching and getting plastered all over the internet.

Take "age verification" laws. There's no such thing as "age verification" – there's just spying on everyone, all the time, creating (even more) records of all of our internet activities:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/19/shes-dead-of-course/#consensus-hallucination

Every promise of "privacy preserving" age verification is bullshit:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/08/14/bellovin/#wont-someone-think-of-the-cryptographers

If you think kids are experiencing internet harms today, just wait until we expose them to the harms of having even more of their data harvested, stored, breached, and weaponized against them:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/06/23/destroy-the-village/#to-save-it

If you want to protect kids from algorithmic manipulation and targeting by bad actors, what about banning spying on kids so no one can target them?

https://made-not-found-by-danah-boyd.ghost.io/no-one-paid-me-to-disagree-with-jonathan-haidt-it-was-teenagers-who-taught-me-that-he-was-wrong/

Now, at this point, you might be thinking, "How can we know who the kids are so we know who not to spy on?" You can't. In order to not spy on kids, you'd just have to not spy on anyone:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/04/09/how-to-make-a-child-safe-tiktok/

"Don't spy on anyone" is the kind of thing that has a reasonable chance of enhancing online privacy. But in the time-honored tradition of "we've tried nothing and we're all out of ideas," governments keep finding ways to make digital privacy worse, for example, by procuring Flock cameras for every lamp-post:

https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/09/high-crime-lmao-how-cops-are-treating-mass-surveillance-joke

And then there's UK Labour: after the success of a pilot program for an incredibly effective and safe privacy-preserving way of analyzing the country's health records for research processes, they commissioned the Goldacre Report to evaluate the possibility of making this permanent:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/03/08/the-fire-of-orodruin/#are-we-the-baddies

After that report was completed and had a chance to be metabolized by policymakers, Labour acted upon it…by throwing it out and handing all of the country's health data to Palantir, a serial mishandler of data and violator of privacy:

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/30/legal-objections-palantir-nhs-platform-handling-data

Here's the scariest thing about bad privacy policy: it has a long fuse. The harms of commercial and private-sector digital surveillance can occur years or even decades after the decision to permit it.

There's a straight line from the post-9/11 decision to encourage public agencies to gather, merge and warehouse data on every person in America, and the ability of ICE ethnic cleansing squads to break down people's doors and drag them off to concentration camps; just as there's a straight line from the decision to do nothing about the breach of every Social Security Number and the later theft of all Social Security data by adolescent DOGE criminals:

https://www.pcmag.com/news/is-your-ssn-in-the-national-public-data-breach-heres-how-to-find-out

But despite how obvious these connections are, the fact that they're separated by a lot of time and space provides our policymakers with cover for making terrible decisions with foreseeably terrible outcomes. As a society, we lack object permanence, the ability to connect acts in the past with present-day phenomena.

When the press reports on a "Black October" of catastrophic, AI-fueled data breaches and hack attacks, they don't mention a generation of policymakers' indifference and hostility to information security:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake

Policymakers benefit from politics' eternal now, in which disasters simply befall us, without any history or precedent or cause. Remember the One Big Beautiful Bill? Its architects designed it to wreak its worst harms after the midterms, with Medicaid work rules and food aid restrictions starting in December, and cuts to affordable housing and rural hospitals phasing in through the year:

https://www.tumblr.com/mostlysignssomeportents/832146932089700352

Black October is going to give way to Black November, Black December, Black 2027, and the Black 2030s – a string of cybersecurity catastrophes that will befall us until policymakers decide that keeping us safe is more important than making it easy for them to attack their chosen "bad guys."

Here's a preview of Black November: there's a new strain of the Volta infostealer malware that uses AI tools to dox you even as it hacks you:

https://www.wired.com/story/kernel-panic-volta-autodoxer-ai-infostealer-malware/

How that works: your computer gets hacked and your data gets stolen, then it gets merged with breach data from Ticketmaster, Disney, AT&T and other companies that have recklessly compiled vast troves of data on all of us, stored it insecurely, and leaked it onto the internet where it will live forever.

Volta's makers prompt their LLM "to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim." This lets the criminals prioritize their victims based on the expected return from exploiting them. It augments this dossier by combing through your Gmail as well as your Doordash and Uber Eats profiles. This merged data makes it much easier for criminals to call you up or email you (or have a chatbot call you up or email you) and trick you into giving up even more data:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/02/05/cyber-dunning-kruger/#swiss-cheese-security

Volta seems especially interested in younger internet users, targeting "Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions." Of course, once our "age verification" services breach vast, eternally persistent, detailed troves of data on young internet users, this kind of AI-supercharged malware will be able to target kids with much greater fidelity and efficacy.

AI capabilities have made infostealers much worse, but the reason for that new potency lies in how AI capabilities are supercharged by breach data that is the foreseeable and foreseen consequence of generations of hostility to privacy on the part of policymakers and corporations who responded to the incentives policymakers created.

We are living in the age of oily rags. For decades we fucked around with letting the private sector warehouse our data and weaken our security so that public sector agencies could plunder our data and our computers at will. Now, we keep finding out that everything is on fire.

It's going to take a long time to fix this, but we can do it. We can build more secure systems. We can make it much more of a legal ball-ache for companies to gather our data in the first place, and we can legalize and promote the creation of privacy blockers for browsers, phones, computers, cars, thermostats and smart speakers. We can enact corporate death-penalties for breaches to reflect the true societal cost of warehousing our data. We can ban Flock cameras and tear down the post-9/11 "fusion centers" that neatly package up our data for use by DOGE fascists and ICE thugs. We can ban our spy agencies from hoarding defects in widely used software, and instead require them to divulge these bugs so vendors can fix them:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOBUS

And before we do any of that, we can just stop making it worse by ending the campaigns to require companies to spy on us and deliberately introduce security defects into their products.

title: Lorem Ipsum Dot Gov Dot UK
content:
I love testing in production. The thrill of accidentally publishing some dummy data - or taking down an entire website - is similar to skydiving without a parachute. Exquisite excitement followed by heart-stopping terror.

Before going live with a new website or service, it's sensible to test how text looks on it. Most people don't test with readable text - it's too easy for management to start reading the content rather than looking at the layout. So the default is the Latin text "Lorem ipsum". Latin looks enough like English to get a feel for how text will render - but most people can't read it so they gloss over the words and look at the layout.

Say, it sure would be annoying if those dummy pages ever made their way to production, right?!?

One of the things that's fascinating about seeing testing data in a live environment is that you get a small peek behind the curtain of how a site was made. A tiny glimpse into the minds of the people who made it.

Who was Alice? Did she enjoy her time working on the London Councils' website?

Was she friends with Henry at Lambeth council? We may never know.

Some of the placeholders eventually become load-bearing. For reasons which remain inscrutable to those who follow, the Elders declared some pages must remain sacrosanct forever!

What would happen if that page were deleted? Would you dare risk it?

Sometimes finding a test page leads to a dead end. A stub of a page which should have been purged before go-live.

But other times it can lead us to a page hinting at something more. Deeper tests of long-forgotten functionality.

What did those plugins do? Aaaaaaaa indeed!

The purpose of this post isn't to point and laugh, it's to show that searching for dummy data is a good way to find interesting things. It might show you a style-guide, or lead to you to a forgotten and outdated plugin, or it might lead you to an entire pre-production environment.

Finally, this image was on one of the FCDO blog posts. I assume that means it is available under the Open Government Licence and, therefore, I can start T-Shirt production immediately!

title: Sneaking into the auditorium for the Windows 2000 launch rehearsal
content:
The Windows 2000 launch in San Francisco was accompanied by an expo, and a large number of Windows 2000 team members were dispatched to run the various booths and stations, give informal presentations on the new features of Windows 2000, and answer technical questions from the various attendees. And from among the people who were sent to the expo, a smaller group was selected to attend the launch event itself in person.

Related reading: A ticket to the Windows 95 launch.

After a few of us arrived early at the Civic Auditorium for the launch event, we had to entertain ourselves until the doors opened. There was some speculation as to who the celebrity host would be, since it hadn’t been announced. One of my colleagues tried to sneak into what looked like a VIP tent.¹ I, on the other hand, went exploring.

I found an unlocked door that took me into the empty upper level of the main auditorium.

I took a seat and tried not to be noticed.

The stage was set up with a 10-meter tall mock laptop, screens to the left and right of the stage for projecting slides, prerecorded videos, or to get a better look at on-stage close-ups, gray curtains unobtrusively hung to shield from view what would turn out to be various surprises throughout the event, and various other desks, demo areas, and even an airplane cabin set.²

While I sat and took in the complexity of the stage, there was an announcement that they would be rehearsing the opening in one minute. The lights dimmed in preparation. The lid of the giant laptop closed very slowly.

About ten minutes after the announcement, the rehearsal actually began.

The laptop lid opened, and on the laptop screen, it looked like someone was signing into Windows 2000, and then the mouse clicked the Start button. This led to a video montage, and when the montage was over, a voice announced, “Ladies and Gentlemen, please welcome Patrick Stewart!”

Oh my goodness, Patrick Stewart is going to be the presenter for the Windows 2000 launch!

Mere seconds later, onto the stage bounded… a crew member wearing a headset pretending to be Patrick Stewart so that the camera and lighting crew could make sure they were properly positioned.

Okay, that’s the end of the rehearsal. The lights come back on, and the auditorium once again buzzes with the sound of equipment being moved and people discussing things.

I left the auditorium and went back to join the crowd of people waiting to get in. I didn’t tell them who the host was.

The event itself seemed to go off pretty much as planned. With the real Patrick Stewart.

Patrick Stewart had such a commanding presence. If he had come out on stage and announced, “It is the dawn of a new era: The era of lime Jell-O”, people would say, “Yeah, lime Jell-O, I need to upgrade to lime Jell-O.” But instead of trying to spark a new dessert trend, he talked about Windows 2000, reading words from a teleprompter that he almost certainly didn’t understand, but he made them sound great.

¹ My colleague eventually returned with a Commemorative Edition boxed copy of Windows 2000.

² The airplane cabin was used for a sketch that demonstrated mobile business computing. The demoer took their laptop on a plane trip, where they happened to sit next to a character named William Wentworth, portrayed by actor John O’Hurley, president of William Wentworth Worldwide. (He gave his email address as www@www.com.) The sketch demonstrated infrared file sharing and other mobile scenarios. Remember infrared file sharing? Of course you don’t.

The post Sneaking into the auditorium for the Windows 2000 launch rehearsal appeared first on The Old New Thing.

title: Making peace with the projective plane
content:
In my newsletter I give an introduction to the latest few posts and occasionally give some additional commentary. In my latest newsletter I wrote

Projective space and homogeneous coordinates seemed like arbitrary abstractions when I was a student because they were presented without any motivation. Much later I came to realize that they’re natural, almost inevitable. Exceptional cases and hand-wavy references to objects “at infinity” go away when moving to projective space.

My mathematics education was very top-down: abstractions first, specifics later (if ever). I was OK with that for a while, until I hit my abstraction tolerance sometime in grad school. Now I would advocate more of a bottom-up approach, motivating abstractions first rather than presenting them as a fait acompli.

The first time I saw the projective plane was probably in a topology class where someone said you could construct the plane by starting with a square and gluing opposite edges in a physically impossible way. This seemed like a gimmick, a way to construct a non-orientable manifold but not anything practical. Another construction is to say the projective plane is an ordinary sphere with antipodal points identified. I found that a little more satisfying, but it still unmotivated.

What I would have appreciated was someone saying that the projective plane was invented to make geometry more elegant by eliminating exceptional cases and making rigorous the idea of things “at infinity.” For example, geometric calculations often have to treat vertical lines specially, but vertical lines are not special in projective geometry.

You could start by saying we’re going to represent points in the plane not simply as (x, y) but as (x, y, 1) and use (x, y, 0) for the point at infinity in the direction (x, y). That may seem like a hack, but it’s certainly motivated. It’s exactly the sort of thing a graphics programmer would do. In fact, I imagine many programmers have done just that, independently bumping into projective geometry.

After having introduced this extra coordinate, it’s natural to ask what would it mean if the last coordinate were something other than 0 or 1. You’ll quickly run into this when you start doing calculations on these extended coordinates. You could have a rule that you always normalize by dividing by the last coordinate, if it’s not zero, and then you have essentially discovered homogeneous coordinates.

You’ll see something like the approach above in elliptic curve cryptography. Programmers wanting to implement encryption algorithms are thinking concretely in terms of (x, y) points, until they have to worry about a mysterious “point at infinity” and handle it correctly. Then homogenous coordinates appear as a tool for getting out of a bind.

***

I thought about titling this post something like “Dr. Stragelove, or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and and Love the Projective Plane” but I wasn’t sure how well that would go over. I doubt many readers have seen the 1964 movie this is alluding to, but the trope “How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love …” is more widely known than the movie itself.

The post Making peace with the projective plane first appeared on John D. Cook.

title: Pray for Chaos
content:
There’s two basic ways AI can play out, one is order, the other is chaos.

Order is the very dangerous one. If it turns out that models are actually capable of patching all the exploits, it’s hard to imagine what will disrupt the status quo. Fortunately, this seems unlikely, but that doesn’t mean order won’t prevail in the short term. At the end of my Yudkowsky debate we found a tangible point of disagreement. He thinks AI will be able to find a solution to the Prisoner’s dilemma. I know there already is a solution (it’s defect), EA people just aren’t happy about it.

If it won’t be order (and you better pray it won’t be order) that leaves chaos. AI that can play a whole society in hours can manufacture entire histories, years of archives of daily newspapers, and an Internet that never happened. The dead Internet theory is coming true before our eyes. Now I can still see the bots, soon I won’t be able to. Scratch that, I probably already often can’t.


Gwern wrote about this, it’s hard to imagine a vision of humans as prompters or enter pressers in 2030. The US AI companies don’t believe they have to offer any solution to this, why would they have to justify in any way that their products are good for society? Anthropic cannot wait until they have the leverage to ban all their users. Why would you keep around the middle man?

Here’s the most positive vision I can come up with. If it turns out things can’t be secured, we enter an era of increased decentralization. Think everyone running their own custom different OS, not everyone running the same version of Linux on a computer they can touch. Because the centralized homogeneous systems are too vulnerable. Cyber attacks flying in every direction, nobody capable of keeping infrastructure up, cars sitting in driveways as bricks (or worse, rooted to steer you off a cliff).

Self replicating AI hiding out in every corner of every hard drive. How powerful of a model do you need for it to stand a chance of reproduction in today’s cyberworld? GLM-5.2 and up?

A media landscape that is botted and microtargeted to all hell, nonsensical elections where the only thing people agree on is the names of candidates. Massive dumps of corporate slacks and intranets. (come on Russian kids, grab an abliterated AI and do a hacking!)

Whatever you hold dear the chaos army will come for too. The Internet era is over. Your life will never be the same. The chaos will come for the resistance as well as the fascists; it’s unclear who it will hurt more. Your life plan is probably already nonsense in the face of AI. Mine sort of is. What economic value you think you will have in 10 years? Who will be around for you to have that value to? Do you think you’ll be able to make any sense of the world?


And remember, chaos is the good outcome. The alternative is that you are a dancing monkey in a cage you won’t be smart enough to see.
description: There’s two basic ways AI can play out, one is order, the other is chaos.
